Stock and bond prices edged higher in cautious trading Monday ahead of Tuesday's national elections.
The dollar ended mixed, lumber prices soared to the highest level in nearly three years and crude oil fell.

The Dow Jones industrial average added 19.75 points to 6,041.68 as a string of mergers energised individual stocks. In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,331 to 1,040 on active volume of 391 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

"The markets are doing well prior to the election on the assumption (President) Clinton will be re-elected and we'll have nothing worse than a narrowing of the majority in Congress that Republicans will have," said Allen Sinai, chief economist at Lehman Brothers Global Economic Advisors.

Buyers also lifted bonds, with the bellwether 30-year Treasury bond adding nearly a quarter point, lowering its yield, which moves in the opposite direction from the price, to 6.66 percent from 6.68 percent at Friday's close.

"The bond market is poised to do better if the elections turn out okay," said Sinai, who projects a modest selloff should the Democrats sweep and win the White House and take control of both houses of Congress.
Clinton's re-election was considered nearly certain, but investors feared a Democrat sweep of the House and Senate that could unleash lead to higher taxes and more government spending.

"Bonds are concerned that a Democratic sweep will result in massive social spending and an upward explosion in the size of the deficit which will drive inflation higher and bond prices lower," said Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management.
Other than the elections, Wall Street also focused on mergers.

MCI Communications rose 50 cents to $30.75 on news that it would be acquired by British Telecommunications Plc for $20 billion -- the biggest trans-Atlantic deal ever. Analysts said regulatory hurdles for the deal and a lengthy 12 months to complete it limited the rise in MCI's stock. British Telecom's American shares jumped $6.125 to $61.625 on the NYSE.
In currency markets, the dollar ended mixed Monday in quiet, mostly featureless trading ahead of the presidential and congressional elections on Tuesday.

"It's a very docile, quiet day," said Tom Benfer, director of foreign exchange at Bank of Montreal. "I think it's keeping people on the sidelines from taking big positions," he said, referring to the elections.
The dollar rose to 113.80 Japanese yen late in New York, from 113.35 yen late Friday. The dollar fell to 1.5105 German marks from 1.5143 marks.
The British pound kept rising and settled at $1.6453, up from $1.6360 late Friday.
Lumber prices rose after Canada curtailed exports to the United States to comply with a new trade agreement.

November lumber jumped $28.50 to $477.50 for 1,000 board feet at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, capping a rise of $65, or 16 percent, since Wednesday. It was the highest since the nearby contract reached $488 for 1,000 board feet in December 1993.
Canada on Thursday suspended some exports for two days to control the flow of wood to the United States under the trade pact that took effect on April 1.
December crude oil fell 24 cents to $22.79 a barrel at the New York Mercantile Exchange.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100-stock index closed 20.4 points lower at 3,928.1. The Tokyo stock market was closed for a holiday.
